extracted.intended_audience: graduate research students (science subjects) and their supervisors at NUI Galway
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for planning, writing, formatting and submitting a scientific-style Masters or PhD thesis, aimed at helping graduate students meet examiners' expectations and university regulations. Covers organization, style, grammar, submission rules and examiner assessment criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of the thesis
rubrics_metrics.description: The purpose of writing a thesis is to demonstrate to an academic readership that you are competent in conducting and writing up a significant body of research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You must communicate research at the appropriate level to experts, plan, write and revise drafts, and produce a finished version suitable for assessment and possible publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of the central research question
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners expect a succinct, straightforward declarative statement of the central research question/hypothesis, presented in the Abstract and at the start of the thesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the central research question plainly so examiners immediately grasp the core of your research; the Abstract is the linchpin of the thesis' claim to originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Achievement of aims and objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners check that aims/objectives described in the Introduction are explicitly addressed in Results and discussed in the Discussion so the thesis is coherent, not a disjointed set of sections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain correlation between research questions, experiments, results and discussion to ensure a clear line of thought throughout the thesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodology: justification and evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Materials and Methods must justify the chosen methodology and allow examiners to assess why it was chosen, how it provides new information, originality, possible improvements, and limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Answer: Why this methodology? How does it add new information? In what ways is it original? Could it be improved? What are its major/minor limitations?

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality
rubrics_metrics.description: A key criterion: the thesis must make an original contribution to knowledge; results must be new and not already present in the primary literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originality can take many forms (listed in guide): push topic into new areas; original contribution in topic/method/design/theory; solve significant problem or gather original data; reframe issues; imaginative yet rigorous approaches; new theoretical linkages; open neglected areas; leading-edge innovation; personal synthesis; depth and breadth of scholarship; argue against conventions; apply techniques to novel patterns or devise new techniques, etc. Thinking about these helps ensure originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of the field / Literature review
rubrics_metrics.description: The thesis must display sound and thorough understanding of important scholarly work relevant to the research; the literature review should evaluate the literature and relate it to the thesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful literature review evaluates (not merely cites) sources and links the material to your own research; examiners check bibliography to judge mastery of the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree-specific examination criteria (Research Master's)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a research Master’s, candidate must demonstrate a contribution to understanding/knowledge, appropriate depth and breadth of understanding, and expertise in relevant methodologies and techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners will look for evidence of these in the thesis; oral exam is not normally required. Master’s theses should not exceed 45,000 words (inclusive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree-specific examination criteria (PhD)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a PhD, candidate must have made a significant contribution to knowledge, produced work suitable for publication (in whole or part), displayed depth and breadth of knowledge, and gained significant methodological expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners look for these in the thesis and viva is critical to confirm standards. PhD thesis should not normally exceed 80,000 words (inclusive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adhere to University submission rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Candidates must follow the University Guidelines for Research Degree Programmes with respect to format, layout and presentation before submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check the full rules in the official guidelines; the manual highlights key layout requirements but is not a substitute for the official document.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title page contents
rubrics_metrics.description: A thesis title page must contain: full title (and subtitle), total number of volumes and volume number (if applicable), full name of author (as registered), qualification sought, supervisor(s) and school/discipline/institution, and month/year of submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The title should accurately and concisely describe thesis content; the name on the thesis must match the registered name exactly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copies, forms and abstract on submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific numbers of copies and accompanying forms/abstracts are required on submission (varies for Research Master's and PhD and for medical degrees).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research Master’s: two (or three) copies with completed EOG 052 and abstract ≤300 words; PhD: two copies with 'Summary of Contents' ≤300 words and EOG 020; final bound copy and electronic copy submission requirements also apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical formatting: paper, margins, spacing, font
rubrics_metrics.description: Text should be printed on good quality 110 grams A4 paper with left-hand margin 4 cm; maximum one-and-a-half line spacing; left-justified; 12 point font recommended; double-sided printing recommended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use readable layout; adhere strictly to spacing and margin requirements to avoid formatting objections from examiners/administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pagination and numbering conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Pages must be numbered consecutively; page numbers located centrally at the bottom and chapter headers at the top; page numbers should start in Chapter 1 with Arabic numerals and earlier sections with Roman numerals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the convention to help examiners navigate the thesis easily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figures and tables: placement and numbering
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures and tables should be located adjacent to related text and numbered correctly with chapter number and sequence number (e.g., figure 4.3 is third figure in chapter 4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use similar conventions for tables; ensure captions and numbering are consistent and sequential in each chapter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binding and final submission format
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial submission copies should be spiral or gum bound; final copy must be hard-bound with leaves permanently secured and have cover/spine information (title, candidate, degree, date). An electronic copy must also be submitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow specific binding requirements (different for Masters/PhD/medical degrees) and submit required Library Submission Form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Back up files and software settings
rubrics_metrics.description: Back up files regularly using multiple methods (email attachments, removable disks, external drives) and set word-processing language to UK English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid loss of work; check institutional IT guidance on network storage and backup procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtain and study successful theses
rubrics_metrics.description: Find copies of successful theses in your area to observe structure, chapter length, useful phrases and presentation conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use them as models but remember no thesis is perfect and your work must be original.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-writing activities and outlining
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize references in the order you will use them, create an outline of the thesis agreed with your supervisor, and make plans for each section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List points to cover, arrange order, and supplement outlines with detailed plans for sections to make writing easier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make time to write / write regularly
rubrics_metrics.description: Schedule and block out regular time for writing in your weekly calendar; writing is an integral part of your research and should be practiced frequently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose times that fit your alertness patterns; treat writing as essential, not optional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write in brief bursts
rubrics_metrics.description: Break large writing tasks into smaller chunks and tackle them in short, timed sessions to maintain concentration and motivation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use timed deadlines for sessions to help sustain momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set and keep personal deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Set concrete deadlines for sections and stick to them, possibly agreeing deadlines with your supervisor and rewarding milestones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use external motivators (e.g., no holiday until a chunk is finished) to maintain progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing vs revising: separate tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep writing and revising separate: writing sessions should focus on producing new text, while editing, formatting and checking references should be done in separate sessions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you need to note something for later, jot it and continue writing to maintain momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start writing from the beginning of research
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep daily written records (lab notebooks) and begin thinking about/starting thesis writing from the start of postgraduate study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure lab notebooks contain all info needed for the thesis; writing helps formulate and reflect on ideas and track progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overcoming writer’s block
rubrics_metrics.description: Use techniques such as relaxation, planning, mind-maps, brainstorming, writing tables/figures first, and short drafting to overcome blocks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brainstorm imperfectly, get words down physically, use diagrams/mind maps to clarify structure, bring techniques tried to supervisor if help is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acting on feedback and iterative revision
rubrics_metrics.description: Use feedback from supervisors and colleagues to redraft while suggestions are fresh; treat thesis writing as a multi-stage drafting process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Print drafts for different perspective, perform close edits to remove spelling/grammar/typos, check paragraph linkage and coherence, and systematically rework drafts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish ground rules with your supervisor
rubrics_metrics.description: Agree expectations at the start (broad issues and matters of style) so supervision is effective and writing proceeds smoothly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss frequency of meetings, feedback turnaround, preferred writing conventions, authorship expectations, and use provided tables as prompts for discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis organisation: Introduction (including Literature Review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduction should state aims/objectives, introduce the central question and include a literature review that evaluates and relates prior work to your thesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the purpose and contribution clear; ensure literature review shows mastery and links to your research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis organisation: Materials and Methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe methods thoroughly so experiments are reproducible and methodology choices are justified and their limitations discussed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be clear about experimental design, protocols, controls, and any novel methodological approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis organisation: Results
rubrics_metrics.description: Present findings clearly and objectively, using figures and tables appropriately; results chapters should address the stated objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid interpretation-heavy language in Results; reserve synthesis and broader meaning for the Discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis organisation: Discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret results, relate them to the central research question and literature, discuss implications, limitations and future work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure Discussion ties back to aims/objectives and synthesizes theoretical and empirical findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis organisation: Bibliography/References
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a comprehensive bibliography of works consulted and follow the required referencing style consistently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For scientific theses, Harvard is normal; confirm with supervisor/School; correct citation practice demonstrates scholarship and avoids plagiarism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract: purpose and length
rubrics_metrics.description: The Abstract is a key page introducing the thesis, explaining the central hypothesis and providing the vital points by which the thesis will be assessed; typically limited to 300 words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the Abstract lucid and declarative; it should be the acid test of the author's grasp and claim to originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other front/back matter: acknowledgements, declarations, TOC, appendices
rubrics_metrics.description: Include standard supporting sections such as acknowledgements, declaration regarding the work, Table of Contents (not over-detailed), list of abbreviations/glossary, and appendices as needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow university conventions for ordering and content of these sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headings and subheadings: consistency and hierarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: Use clear, consistent headings and subheadings to structure the thesis and aid reader navigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow university/School style for heading levels and formatting; ensure Table of Contents reflects the hierarchy without being overly detailed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Font size and style
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a readable font; 12 point font size is recommended for body text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a standard serif or sans-serif font familiar in academic writing and maintain consistency throughout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: A maximum of one-and-a-half line spacing is recommended; left-justify text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow spacing rules and ensure consistent paragraph spacing, indentation and alignment throughout the document.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrations: figures and graphs
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures/graphs should be clear, located adjacent to related text, and properly numbered with captions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure high-quality images, axis labels, legends, and that figures can be understood without excessive text; adhere to chapter-based numbering (e.g., figure 4.3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Tables should be located adjacent to related text, numbered correctly with chapter-based numbering and formatted for readability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use consistent table style, include clear column/row headings and explanatory notes where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of numbers and numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow conventions about when to use words vs numerals (referenced in Table 7.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt the recommended numeric style for consistency (e.g., spell out small numbers where appropriate, use numerals for measurements and data).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific writing: sentences and vocabulary
rubrics_metrics.description: Write to communicate clearly; readers should notice content not style. Use precise vocabulary and well-constructed sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ornate phrasing; prefer clarity and simplicity; consult peer-reviewed articles in your field for presentation style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraphing and coherence
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure paragraphs are well-structured and linked to each other so chapters and the thesis present a coherent argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check paragraph flow during revision; each paragraph should have a clear topic and link to surrounding text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verb tense consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Use appropriate and consistent verb tenses (guidance provided in section on verb tenses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose tenses appropriate to context (e.g., present for general facts, past for methods/results) and keep them consistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid double negatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Double negatives should be avoided in academic writing to prevent ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to Table 8.1 for examples of how to avoid double negatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful use of 'only'
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of 'only' can change sentence meaning; follow recommended usages to avoid ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Table 8.2 for different placements of 'only' and how meaning shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'to comprise'
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific guidance given on correct usage of 'to comprise' to avoid common errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to Table 8.3 for correct phrasing and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use abbreviations sparingly; define them on first use and include a list of abbreviations/glossary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overloading text with unexplained acronyms; maintain consistency and ensure abbreviations aid readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid commonly confused words
rubrics_metrics.description: Be vigilant about commonly confused pairs/triples (there/their/they’re, affect/effect/impact, fewer/less, among/between, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult provided tables (8.4–8.12 etc.) and proofread carefully to avoid these errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Academic tone: avoid jargon and slang
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain an academic, professional tone; avoid informal language, slang and excessive discipline-specific jargon without explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for clarity; explain necessary technical terms and avoid unnecessary complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity and avoiding wordiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Be concise: avoid wordy phrases and excess words; aim for succinct writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult tables on wordy phrases to avoid and techniques for omitting excess words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid contractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Contractions are too informal for academic writing and should generally be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use full forms (do not → do not) to maintain formal tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender-neutral language
rubrics_metrics.description: Use gender-neutral terms and avoid outdated gendered language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See tables on gender-neutral equivalents and how to avoid misuse of ‘his’.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key punctuation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Use punctuation correctly: guidance on apostrophe, brackets, capitals, colon, comma, dash, ellipsis, exclamation marks (avoid), full stop, italics, question mark, quotation marks and semi-colon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to alphabetical list of punctuation in 8.6.1 for precise examples and anti-patterns (e.g., do not use exclamation marks in academic writing; use single quotes for quotations; semi-colons to join independent clauses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spelling vigilance
rubrics_metrics.description: Use spellcheckers but manually verify specialist technical terms and commonly confused spellings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Add correct technical terms to dictionary if needed; create a glossary of specialist words; consult Table 8.21 for common misspellings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof-reading checklists: content
rubrics_metrics.description: Checklist to confirm text is objective, structured correctly, examples relevant, sources referenced and facts accurate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Table 8.22 checklist before submitting chapters to supervisor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof-reading checklists: style
rubrics_metrics.description: Checklist to ensure aims/objectives are clear, meaning is consistent, text is signposted and fluent, informal language removed, academic style maintained, tense consistent and section lengths balanced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Table 8.23 as a practical editing aid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof-reading checklists: grammar
rubrics_metrics.description: Checklist to ensure sentences are accurate, paragraphing consistent, grammar-checker suggestions addressed and text read aloud to catch errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Table 8.24 and a good grammar reference to enforce standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof-reading checklists: spelling and punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Checklist to correct typos, run spellcheck, verify specialist terms, double-check punctuation and capitalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Table 8.25 to systematically sweep for errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof-reading checklists: presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Checklist to ensure text fits word counts, is neatly presented, pages numbered, figures/tables formatted, bibliography comprehensive and citation practice accurate, and spacing follows guidelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Table 8.26 to create strong first impressions with examiners through meticulous presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation practice and academic integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Correct citation practice is a test of scholarship: acknowledge sources, chart intellectual influences, and follow required referencing style (Harvard typical in sciences). Any type of plagiarism is unacceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check School/supervisor for required style, consult library guides, and follow University plagiarism policy; maintain accurate, consistent referencing throughout.
